questions.stem:
Choose the correct passive voice form of the sentence:
Active: 'The boy kicks the ball.'

options.option_text: The ball was kicked by the boy.
The ball is kicked by the boy.
The ball has been kicked by the boy.
The ball is being kicked by the boy.

questions.explanation: The active sentence is in the simple present tense. The passive structure for simple present is: Subject + is/am/are + Past Participle (V3) + by + Object. 'The ball is kicked by the boy.'

questions.stem:
Choose the correct passive voice form of the sentence:
Active: 'She wrote a beautiful letter.'

options.option_text: A beautiful letter is written by her.
A beautiful letter had been written by her.
A beautiful letter was written by her.
A beautiful letter will be written by her.

questions.explanation: The active sentence is in the simple past tense. The passive structure for simple past is: Subject + was/were + Past Participle (V3) + by + Object. 'A beautiful letter was written by her.'

questions.stem:
Choose the correct passive voice form of the sentence:
Active: 'They are painting the old wall.'

options.option_text: The old wall was being painted by them.
The old wall has been painted by them.
The old wall is painted by them.
The old wall is being painted by them.

questions.explanation: The active sentence is in the present continuous tense. The passive structure is: Subject + is/am/are + being + Past Participle (V3) + by + Object. 'The old wall is being painted by them.'

questions.stem:
Choose the correct passive voice form of the sentence:
Active: 'Someone has stolen my expensive pen.'

options.option_text: My expensive pen has been stolen.
My expensive pen was stolen.
My expensive pen is stolen.
My expensive pen had been stolen.

questions.explanation: The active sentence is in the present perfect tense. The passive structure is: Subject + has/have + been + Past Participle (V3). When the agent ('someone') is vague, 'by someone' is typically omitted. 'My expensive pen has been stolen.'

questions.stem:
Choose the correct passive voice form of the imperative sentence:
Active: 'Open the door immediately.'

options.option_text: The door should be opened immediately.
The door must be opened immediately.
Let the door be opened immediately.
Let the door open immediately.

questions.explanation: For imperative sentences expressing an order or command, the passive structure generally starts with 'Let', followed by the object, then 'be', and finally the past participle. 'Let the door be opened immediately.'

questions.stem:
Choose the correct passive voice form of the interrogative sentence:
Active: 'Who taught you English so well?'

options.option_text: By whom are you taught English so well?
By whom were you taught English so well?
By whom was English taught you so well?
By who were you taught English so well?

questions.explanation: The sentence is in the simple past tense. In interrogative sentences starting with 'Who', the passive form begins with 'By whom', followed by the auxiliary verb (were), the subject (you), and the past participle (taught).

questions.stem:
Choose the correct passive voice form of the sentence:
Active: 'People clearly say that he is a foreign spy.'

options.option_text: It was clearly said that he was a foreign spy.
People are clearly saying that he is a foreign spy.
He was clearly said to be a foreign spy.
It is clearly said that he is a foreign spy.

questions.explanation: Sentences starting with 'People say', 'They believe', etc., can be transformed into passive voice by using the introductory 'It'. Since 'say' is in the present tense, the passive form is 'It is said'. 'It is clearly said that he is a foreign spy.'

questions.stem: Which option correctly transforms 'The coach will train the players rigorously this season' into passive voice?

options.option_text: The players will train rigorously by the coach this season.
The players will be trained rigorously by the coach this season.
The players would be trained rigorously by the coach this season.
The players will have been trained rigorously by the coach this season.

questions.explanation: B is correct because future simple passive = 'will + be + past participle': 'will be trained'. Option A keeps the active infinitive 'will train' without 'be', so it remains active. Option C substitutes 'would' for 'will', introducing an unwarranted conditional meaning. Option D applies future perfect passive ('will have been trained'), which implies completion before a future reference point — a tense not present in the original.

questions.stem: Which option gives the correct passive voice of 'The chef was preparing a special dish for the guests'?

options.option_text: A special dish was prepared for the guests by the chef.
A special dish had been prepared for the guests by the chef.
A special dish was being prepared for the guests by the chef.
A special dish is being prepared for the guests by the chef.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Past continuous passive = 'was/were + being + past participle'. The active 'was preparing' (past continuous) becomes 'was being prepared'. Option A uses simple past passive ('was prepared'), losing the continuous aspect. Option B uses past perfect passive ('had been prepared'), which is a different tense altogether. Option D shifts to present continuous passive ('is being prepared'), changing the tense from past to present.

questions.stem: Select the correct passive voice of 'Every citizen must obey the laws of the country'. Which option is accurate?

options.option_text: The laws of the country must have been obeyed by every citizen.
The laws of the country must be obeyed by every citizen.
The laws of the country must be obeying by every citizen.
The laws of the country should be obeyed by every citizen.

questions.explanation: B is correct. For sentences with modal verbs, passive = 'modal + be + past participle': 'must obey' → 'must be obeyed'. Option A uses 'must have been obeyed' (modal perfect), implying a past obligation already fulfilled — a different construction entirely. Option C wrongly uses 'be obeying' (present participle) instead of the past participle 'obeyed'. Option D substitutes 'should' for 'must', changing the degree of obligation and altering the original meaning.

questions.stem: Which passive transformation of 'The manager did not approve the revised budget proposal' is correct?

options.option_text: The revised budget proposal is not approved by the manager.
The revised budget proposal has not been approved by the manager.
The revised budget proposal was not approved by the manager.
The revised budget proposal was not being approved by the manager.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The active uses simple past negative ('did not approve'); simple past passive = 'was/were + not + past participle' → 'was not approved'. The auxiliary 'did' is a simple past marker, not a separate tense signal in the passive. Option A shifts to simple present passive ('is not approved'), wrong tense. Option B uses present perfect passive ('has not been'), again wrong tense. Option D uses past continuous passive ('was not being approved'), which misrepresents the original as an ongoing past action.

questions.stem: Which passive form correctly transforms 'The government awarded the scientist a prestigious national honour'?

options.option_text: The scientist was awarded to a prestigious national honour by the government.
The scientist was awarded a prestigious national honour by the government.
The scientist had been awarded a prestigious national honour by the government.
The scientist is awarded a prestigious national honour by the government.

questions.explanation: B is correct. With ditransitive verbs like 'award', when the indirect object (scientist) becomes the passive subject, the direct object (honour) is retained without any preposition: 'The scientist was awarded a prestigious national honour'. Option A erroneously inserts 'to' after 'awarded', which would only be correct if the direct object were the subject ('A prestigious national honour was awarded to the scientist'). Option C applies past perfect passive, altering the tense. Option D uses simple present passive, ignoring the original simple past.

questions.stem: Which option gives the correct passive transformation of 'The authorities looked into the matter immediately after the complaint'?

options.option_text: The matter was looked by the authorities into immediately after the complaint.
The matter has been looked into by the authorities immediately after the complaint.
The matter was looked at by the authorities immediately after the complaint.
The matter was looked into by the authorities immediately after the complaint.

questions.explanation: D is correct. 'Look into' is an inseparable phrasal verb meaning 'investigate'; the particle 'into' must remain attached to 'looked' in the passive: 'was looked into by the authorities'. Option A wrongly splits the phrasal verb, placing 'into' after the agent phrase ('looked by the authorities into'), which is ungrammatical. Option B shifts to present perfect passive ('has been looked into'), changing the tense. Option C substitutes 'looked at' (to examine visually) — an entirely different phrasal verb that alters the meaning of the sentence.

questions.stem: Which option correctly transforms 'By the time he arrives, the culprits will have disposed of all evidence' into passive voice?

options.option_text: By the time he arrives, all evidence will have disposed of by the culprits.
By the time he arrives, all evidence will be disposed of by the culprits.
By the time he arrives, all evidence will have been disposed of by the culprits.
By the time he arrives, all evidence would have been disposed of by the culprits.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Future perfect passive = 'will + have + been + past participle'. 'Will have disposed of' → 'will have been disposed of'; the particle 'of' (from the phrasal verb 'dispose of') is retained after the past participle. Option A omits the essential auxiliary 'been' ('will have disposed of' — this is active future perfect, not passive). Option B uses future simple passive ('will be disposed of'), dropping 'have' and thus losing the future perfect aspect. Option D substitutes 'would' for 'will', converting a factual future prediction into an unwarranted conditional.
